title: Mortgage Company Insurance Claim Check: How to Get It Released
description: Insurance check made out to you and your lender? Learn how the mortgage company insurance claim check process works and how to get funds released faster.
html:
You finally received payment on your storm or fire claim, and then you notice your lender's name is on it too. A mortgage company insurance claim check is one of the most frustrating parts of the claim process for Galveston homeowners, because the money is technically yours to rebuild with, but you cannot deposit it without the lender's signature. This guide explains why lenders are named on the check, how the endorsement and release process usually works, and what you can do to keep repairs moving.

Why Your Mortgage Company Is on the Insurance Claim Check

Nearly every mortgage requires you to insure the home and name the lender as a "mortgagee" or "loss payee" on the policy. The home is the lender's collateral. When the insurer pays for damage to the dwelling, it is required by the policy's mortgage clause to include the lender as a payee. Payments for contents (personal property) and additional living expenses are often issued to you alone, but dwelling payments almost always include the lender.

This applies to TWIA windstorm payments, private homeowners policies, and NFIP flood payments. If you have more than one mortgage or a home equity line, you may see more than one lender on the check.

How the Mortgage Company Insurance Claim Check Process Usually Works

Each servicer has its own rules for handling a mortgage company insurance claim check, but the process follows a similar pattern:

  1. You endorse the check. Sign the back as the named insured. Every named insured on the check must sign.
  2. You contact the servicer's loss draft department. Large servicers have a dedicated "loss draft" or "insurance claims" team. Your regular customer service line can transfer you. Ask for a claim number with the lender.
  3. You send the check and required documents. The lender endorses it and deposits it into a restricted escrow or loss draft account, or for smaller amounts may endorse and return it to you.
  4. The lender releases funds in stages. For larger claims, funds are often released as draws: an initial portion to start work, additional draws after inspections, and a final release when repairs are complete.
  5. A final inspection closes the file. The lender may send an inspector or accept photos and a completion certificate from your contractor.

Documents Lenders Commonly Ask For

Having these ready before you call saves weeks:

  • The endorsed insurance check
  • The insurer's adjuster estimate or statement of loss
  • A signed contract with your contractor, including their license or registration, W-9, and proof of insurance
  • A lender-specific "loss draft" form or affidavit (often called a contractor or homeowner certification)
  • Lien waivers from the contractor as funds are released
  • Photos of completed repairs or a request for inspection

Ask the lender to email you its full checklist and put your claim number on every page you send back.

Why Your Loan Status Matters

How quickly funds are released often depends on whether your loan is current. Servicers frequently apply stricter rules, such as holding all funds until repairs are complete and inspected, when a loan is delinquent. Some servicers release smaller claims in full to borrowers who are current. Ask directly: "What is your release policy for my claim amount given my loan status?" Get the answer in writing.

Tips to Get Your Insurance Check Released Faster

  • Call the day you receive the check. Loss draft departments can be slow after a hurricane when thousands of Gulf Coast claims arrive at once.
  • Send everything by trackable method. Overnight with tracking, and keep copies of every page.
  • Keep a call log. Date, time, representative name, and what they said.
  • Coordinate your contractor early. Your contractor will need to complete lender paperwork and provide lien waivers. Choose someone who has worked with loss draft departments before.
  • Ask for an initial draw. Many lenders will release a first portion so work can begin. Ask what triggers each draw.
  • Request inspections promptly. As soon as a phase is done, request the inspection needed for the next release.
  • Escalate in writing if stalled. If a servicer is not responding, a written complaint to the servicer and, if needed, to the appropriate regulator may help.

What If the Check Is Too Small to Cover Repairs?

A common problem with a mortgage company insurance claim check: the lender will not release money until repairs are done, but the insurance payment does not cover the real cost of the repairs. That is a claim problem, not a lender problem. If the insurer's estimate missed damage, underpriced labor and materials for the Galveston market, or left out code-required upgrades, you may need to request a supplement or reopen the claim. Our claim settlement calculator can help you estimate what a claim might look like after deductible and depreciation, and our Galveston local code page covers building requirements that can affect repair costs.

For TWIA claims, recoverable depreciation and supplemental payments may be issued separately. Each new dwelling payment will usually include the lender again, so expect to repeat the endorsement process. See our TWIA claims help page for how windstorm payments are structured.

Checks for Contents and Living Expenses

Payments for personal property and additional living expenses (ALE) are generally meant for you, not for rebuilding the structure. If the insurer mistakenly adds your lender to a contents or ALE check, ask the insurer to reissue it payable to you alone. Explain which coverage the payment is for and reference the claim number.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Depositing the check with a forged or missing lender endorsement. This can create serious problems with your bank and lender.
  • Paying a contractor the full amount up front before work begins.
  • Signing a contractor's "direction to pay" or assignment without understanding it.
  • Assuming the first payment is final. Supplements and depreciation holdbacks may still be owed.
  • Letting the claim sit. Policies and Texas law set deadlines, and TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss.

How a Public Adjuster Can Help

A public adjuster licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance works for the policyholder. Beyond preparing the claim itself, a public adjuster can help you organize the documentation lenders ask for, track supplemental payments, and make sure the total claim reflects the true cost to repair so the money held by your lender is actually enough to finish the job.

Quick Checklist for a Mortgage Company Insurance Claim Check

  • Every named insured has endorsed the check
  • Lender loss draft department contacted and claim number recorded
  • Lender's document checklist received in writing
  • Contractor contract, license or registration, W-9, and insurance gathered
  • Draw schedule and inspection process confirmed
  • Copies and tracking numbers saved for everything mailed
  • Insurer estimate reviewed for missed items before repairs start

faq.q: Why is my mortgage company on my insurance claim check?
faq.a: Your mortgage requires the lender to be named as mortgagee on your policy because the home is their collateral. The policy's mortgage clause requires the insurer to include the lender on dwelling payments.

faq.q: How long does it take a mortgage company to release an insurance check?
faq.a: It varies by servicer, claim size, and loan status. Sending a complete document package right away, requesting an initial draw, and scheduling inspections promptly all help keep things moving.

faq.q: Can I cash an insurance check without my lender signing it?
faq.a: No. If the lender is a named payee, its endorsement is required. If a contents or living expense check was wrongly issued with the lender's name, ask the insurer to reissue it payable to you.
